title: Differential equations and initial conditions
description: Turn a rate law into a trajectory and explain the role of initial conditions.
heading: How does a rule for the next instant determine a whole trajectory?
lead: Rate laws become predictive only when paired with initial data and a valid solution method.
outcomes: Solve separable and first-order linear equations while retaining equilibria.
Interpret initial conditions and test a numerical time step.

blocks.body:
A warm object placed in a cooler room does not usually lose the same number of degrees each minute. Its temperature changes fastest when it is far from the room temperature. Suppose measurements support the following model: the rate of temperature change is proportional to the temperature difference, with a minus sign directing the change toward the room. That statement specifies a rate at every possible temperature; it does not yet give the temperature at a particular time.

A differential equation is this kind of rule for change. A solution is a whole function whose derivative obeys the rule throughout an interval. Many functions may obey the same rule because different experiments can start at different temperatures. An initial condition identifies which member of the family describes our experiment.

This distinction separates three jobs. First choose the physical rate law, stating its assumptions. Then solve its mathematical equation. Finally check whether the resulting trajectory agrees with the regime where the model was justified. Exact algebra cannot rescue an inappropriate rate law. We will use cooling to make these jobs visible, then learn a way to follow an equation numerically when a convenient formula is unavailable.

data.title: Euler follows a tangent, not the whole decay curve
data.caption: For y = exp(−t), the tangent at t = 0 meets y = 0 at t = 1, while the exact curve remains positive. Horizontal scale: 180 units per time; vertical scale: 180 units per y.

blocks.title: 1. A rate law gives a family; initial data select a member
blocks.body:
Let $T(t)$ be the object temperature, let $T_a$ be the constant ambient temperature, and assume $T'=-k(T-T_a)$ with $k>0$. This is a model for a body sufficiently uniform in temperature, over a regime where a constant cooling coefficient is reasonable. Define the temperature difference $y=T-T_a$. Since the ambient temperature is fixed, $y'=-ky$. Here k has units of inverse time, so both sides have units of temperature per time.

For a nonzero y, separate variables: $dy/y=-k\,dt$. Integration gives $\ln|y|=-kt+C$. Exponentiating and allowing either sign yields $y=Ae^{-kt}$. The arbitrary real constant A represents a family of possible starting differences. Initial data $y(0)=y_0$ select $A=y_0$. Direct substitution checks the result: differentiating $y_0e^{-kt}$ produces $-ky_0e^{-kt}$.

We divided by y during the calculation. That operation excludes y = 0, which must be checked separately in the original equation. It is an **equilibrium solution**: an object already at ambient temperature stays there in this model. Our final family happens to include it when A = 0, but that fortunate outcome does not justify skipping the check. For a general separable equation $y'=f(t)g(y)$, every root of g is a candidate equilibrium that division by g can lose.

The solution never crosses equilibrium when its initial difference is nonzero: the exponential is positive and the sign of y stays fixed. A positive difference decays toward zero; a negative difference increases toward zero. After the characteristic time $1/k$, the magnitude has fallen by a factor of e. After $\ln2/k$, it has halved. These are predictions of the assumed law, not definitions of every cooling process.

There is also a geometric reading. At each point $(t,y)$ draw a short segment with slope $-ky$. A solution follows these local directions. This slope field describes the whole family without selecting initial data. A starting point then anchors a trajectory. The field is a useful check: a proposed curve above equilibrium that increases with time cannot satisfy this equation.

blocks.bridge: Start with cooling toward a fixed ambient temperature.
blocks.meaning: A differential equation describes possible trajectories; initial data select one.
blocks.question: Why must y = 0 be checked separately when dividing by y?
blocks.answer: Division excludes zero, even though the original decay equation allows the equilibrium y = 0.

further.question: What is y(0) for y = A exp(−kt)?
Can a nonzero exact decay solution cross zero?
further.answer: No; its exponential factor remains positive.

further.question: What units must k have?
further.answer: Inverse time, so ky has the same units as y'.

blocks.title: 2. An integrating factor turns a linear equation into a product
blocks.body:
Cooling with a time-dependent input leads to equations of the form $y'+p(t)y=q(t)$. This equation is called **linear** because y and its derivative appear to the first power and are not multiplied together; the prescribed coefficients may depend on time. The forcing q may represent a heater. A term such as $y^2$ would change the problem into a nonlinear equation.

The product rule suggests a strategy. If a nonzero multiplier $\mu(t)$ satisfies $\mu'=p\mu$, then
$$(\mu y)'=\mu y'+\mu' y=\mu(y'+py)=\mu q.$$
The difficult-looking left side has become one derivative. Solving for the multiplier gives $\mu=\exp(\int p(t)\,dt)$. A fixed nonzero multiplicative constant in this integrating factor changes no final solution, so we may choose the simplest convenient one.

Integrate from the initial time $t_0$ to the observation time t. The result is
$$y(t)=\frac{\mu(t_0)y(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}\mu(s)q(s)\,ds}{\mu(t)}.$$
The dummy variable s prevents confusion between the integration variable and its upper endpoint. This form displays two contributions: the initial state carried forward and the accumulated effect of forcing. Both are weighted by the dynamics.

For constant k and constant input q, the equation is $y'+ky=q$. The steady value is $q/k$, because setting the derivative to zero balances input with loss. Subtract it: $u=y-q/k$ obeys $u'=-ku$. Hence $y=q/k+(y_0-q/k)e^{-kt}$. This route and the integrating factor give the same answer, but subtracting a constant equilibrium makes the physical interpretation especially clear.

Do not confuse a steady value with an initial value. A solution can approach $q/k$ while starting elsewhere. Nor does the existence of a steady value imply stability: changing the sign of k reverses the exponential behavior. The formula must be interpreted through the signs and units of the physical coefficients.

blocks.meaning: An integrating factor makes the product rule work in reverse.
blocks.question: Why choose μ' = pμ?
blocks.answer: Then (μy)' equals μ(y' + py), converting the linear equation to an integrable derivative.

further.question: What steady value solves y' + ky = q for constants?
further.answer: q/k for nonzero k, by setting y' = 0.

further.question: Is that necessarily the initial value?
further.answer: No; the initial state can differ and produce a transient.

further.question: Does μ need an arbitrary multiplicative constant?
further.answer: No; a nonzero constant cancels when solving for y.

blocks.title: 3. Follow local slopes without pretending they are exact
blocks.body:
For an equation $y'=f(t,y)$, suppose an exact solution exists near $(t_n,y_n)$. The derivative chapter gives a local linear prediction over a short interval h:
$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h f(t_n,y_n),\qquad t_{n+1}=t_n+h.$$
This is forward Euler's method. The computed $y_n$ approximates the true solution at $t_n$; it is not a new exact initial condition for the original experiment. Every step uses the slope at the beginning of the interval and follows its tangent line.

When the solution and rate law are sufficiently smooth, the missing next Taylor term is proportional to $h^2$ for a single step starting from exact data. Over a fixed time interval, roughly $1/h$ steps can accumulate an error proportional to h, under suitable stability bounds. This explains why halving h commonly halves the total error. A finite calculation never becomes exact merely by naming h small. Comparing step sizes and checking the equation's qualitative behavior provide evidence about accuracy.

For decay $y'=-ky$, Euler gives $y_{n+1}=(1-kh)y_n$. The true solution preserves the sign of its initial value. A step with $kh>1$ makes the numerical value change sign; with $kh>2$, its magnitude grows from step to step. That growing numerical oscillation is not a discovery about cooling. It is a failure of the chosen approximation. Taking h smaller than $1/k$ preserves positive decay in this example, though accuracy still requires a more careful comparison.

What ensures a starting point chooses only one trajectory? A useful sufficient condition is that f is continuous nearby and changes at a bounded rate with y there; a continuous partial derivative with respect to y supplies that condition. The existence and uniqueness theorem under these hypotheses is quoted here, not proved. It applies locally; solutions can still leave the domain or diverge at a later time.

Uniqueness matters because two trajectories through the same point would give competing future predictions from identical initial data. It is not guaranteed for every handwritten rate law. The optional sidebar shows a case where a trajectory can wait before departing equilibrium. For ordinary linear equations with continuous coefficients, the needed local conditions hold. This makes initial conditions a reliable selection rule within their interval of validity.

blocks.bridge: Replace an unknown trajectory by short tangent steps.
blocks.meaning: Euler's method is a local approximation whose step size affects stability and accuracy.
blocks.question: For y' = −2y and h = 1, what multiplier does Euler use?
blocks.answer: 1 − 2h = −1, producing alternating values instead of true decay.

further.question: What changes when h is halved in a well-behaved Euler calculation?
further.answer: The global error usually falls approximately by two in the small-step regime.

further.question: Does existence imply uniqueness?
further.answer: No. Additional regularity of the rate law with respect to y is needed.

further.question: How can a graph reveal a numerical failure?
further.answer: Sign crossings or growth that contradict the exact rate law flag unsuitable steps.

blocks.heading: A rate law that permits waiting
blocks.body: For $y'=2\sqrt{|y|}$ with $y(0)=0$, both the identically zero function and the function that is zero until a chosen time a ≥ 0 and then equals $(t-a)^2$ solve the equation for t ≥ 0. At departure, both derivatives are zero. The rate law is continuous but is not locally Lipschitz in y at zero. This example explains why a uniqueness theorem needs more than continuity.

blocks.heading: Local derivatives decide the fate of nearby states
blocks.body:
An autonomous rate law $\dot x=f(x)$ has an equilibrium at $x_*$ when $f(x_*)=0$. To investigate whether a small disturbance grows, write $x=x_*+\delta$. The derivative chapter gives
$$f(x_*+\delta)=f(x_*)+f'(x_*)\delta+\text{smaller terms}.$$
Keeping the leading term yields $\dot\delta\approx f'(x_*)\delta$, so $\delta(t)\approx\delta(0)e^{f'(x_*)t}$. A negative slope pushes disturbances back toward equilibrium; a positive slope amplifies them.

For $\dot x=rx(1-x/K)$ with r and K positive, the equilibria are zero and K. The slopes are r and −r respectively. A small positive population grows away from zero, while a small deviation from K decays. One derivative has turned a nonlinear model into the exponential model already studied.

If the slope is zero, this test is silent. Both $\dot x=-x^3$ and $\dot x=x^3$ have zero slope at zero, but the first points toward equilibrium and the second away from it. The terms discarded by linearisation now decide the answer.

With several state variables, the scalar derivative becomes a Jacobian matrix. Its eigenvectors describe disturbance patterns and its eigenvalues describe their linear evolution. Thus local stability joins the derivative, exponential and eigenvector chapters. The approximation describes nearby trajectories while the neglected nonlinear terms remain small; it is not a global solution of the original system.

data.coreIdea: A differential equation supplies a rate law, while an initial condition selects one trajectory from the family allowed by that law. Solving therefore means understanding both the family of possible motions and the information required to identify one member, while checking for equilibria or solutions lost by algebraic division.
data.widerConnection: This separation between law, state, and numerical approximation governs oscillators, fields, orbital propagation, and response theory. It is also the foundation for asking whether a numerical trajectory is faithful to the law rather than merely visually plausible.
